learn.title: Adding at the front
learn.body: The simplest way to grow a list is to add each new node at the front. Make a node, point its `next` at the current head, then make the head point at the new node. It takes the same few steps every time.

learn.title: Three prepends
learn.body: `list` starts as NULL, an empty list. Each loop pass makes the new node the head.

learn.title: The order matters
learn.body: `n->next = list` must come before `list = n`. If you moved head first, you would lose the rest of the list, with nothing pointing to it. That leaked memory cannot be freed.

learn.title: Tracing the loop
steps: i is 1: new node, next NULL, list points to it
i is 2: new node, next is the node 1, list is now node 2
i is 3: the same, so the list reads 3, 2, 1
Items sit in reverse order of adding

learn.body: `show` and `free_list` are written in the next lesson. The output above is 3 2 1.

questions.prompt: An empty list is represented by...
questions.explanation: With no nodes, there is nothing for head to point to, so it is NULL.

questions.prompt: After adding 1, 2, 3 in that order at the front, which value is first?
questions.explanation: Each new node becomes the head, so the last one added is first.

questions.prompt: When adding at the front, set `n->next` to the old \_\_.
questions.explanation: The new node must point at the rest of the list before head moves.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong if you run `list = n` before `n->next = list`?
questions.explanation: After moving head, the old head is no longer stored anywhere, so n->next would point to itself.

questions.prompt: You add 5, then 6, then 7 at the front. What is the first value in the list?
questions.explanation: The newest node is always at the front.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to add a value at the front.
steps: Point its next at the old head
Make head point at the new node
questions.explanation: Link the new node to the list before changing head.
